title: Failure as a Process: An Anatomy of CLI Coding Agent Trajectories
hook: A 3,843-trajectory autopsy of coding agents finds most failures aren't slips — they're wrong beliefs formed in the first few steps, invisible until it's too late to recover.
key_points: Studied 3,843 CLI coding-agent trajectories from 7 frontier models on 3 scaffolds (OpenHands, MiniSWE, Terminus2) via Terminal-Bench.
Hand-annotated 63,000+ execution steps across 1,794 valid trajectories to trace failure as a process, not just a final verdict.
Most failures are epistemic — wrong beliefs or reasoning about the task/environment — not simple execution mistakes.
Failure onset is early: problems typically take root within the first few execution steps.
Failures stay hidden until recovery is no longer possible — outcome-only checks catch them far too late.
Argues agents need earlier validation and self-checking mid-run, not evaluation that only grades the final outcome.
content_html: When a CLI coding agent fails a task, the failure usually isn't a late stumble — it's a wrong belief the agent forms almost immediately and never corrects. This large-scale study treats failure as a process rather than a single end verdict, and finds the rot sets in early and stays invisible until recovery is no longer an option.
extra_html: Xiangxin Zhao, He Ye, and colleagues collected 3,843 trajectories from seven frontier models running on three agent scaffolds — OpenHands, MiniSWE, and Terminus2 — on Terminal-Bench, then hand-annotated 1,794 complete, valid runs (over 63,000 execution steps) to classify how failures emerge, evolve, and become unrecoverable. Across 14 findings, epistemic errors — wrong beliefs about the code, task, or environment — dominate over pure execution mistakes, and onset is consistently early. The authors argue this makes final-outcome-only evaluation a weak lever for reliability: catching bad beliefs while they're still cheap to fix matters more than grading the finished trajectory. Xiangxin Zhao and colleagues, arXiv, July 2026.

related.title: Doomed from the Start: Predicting Agent Failure Before It Happens
related.hook: An agent that's going to fail often shows it in its hidden activations from round one — long before its actual behavior looks any different. Reading that signal saves nearly half the compute.

related.title: TUA-Bench: Benchmarking General-Purpose Terminal Agents
related.hook: 120 real terminal tasks — from email triage to PhD-level scientific workflows — show even Claude Opus 4.8 tops out around 66%, far from reliable general computer use.

flashcards.prompt: When do most coding-agent failures actually take root, per the study's step-by-step annotation?

choices.text: Within the first few execution steps of the trajectory
Only in the final step, right before the deadline
Evenly spread across the whole trajectory with no pattern

flashcards.explanation_html: The study finds failure onset is early — problems typically begin within the first few steps, long before they become visible.

flashcards.prompt: Why do the authors say final-outcome-only evaluation is insufficient for coding agents?
flashcards.back_html: Failures form early and stay hidden until recovery is no longer possible — by the time an outcome check runs, it's already too late to fix.

choices.text: 3,843 trajectories across 7 models/3 scaffolds, with 1,794 hand-annotated (63k+ steps)
A few dozen manually reviewed transcripts from a single model
Purely synthetic trajectories with no real agent runs
